evidence.text:
Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

gold.abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are an established technique to screen for abnormal cardiac signals. Recent work has established that it is possible to detect arrhythmia directly from the ECG signal using deep learning algorithms. While a few prior approaches with contrastive learning have been successful, the best way to define a positive sample remains an open question. In this project, we investigate several ways to define positive samples, and assess which approach yields the best performance in a downstream task of classifying arrhythmia. We explore spatiotemporal invariances, generic augmentations, demographic similarities, cardiac rhythms, and wave attributes of ECG as potential ways to match positive samples. We then evaluate each strategy with downstream task performance, and find that learned representations invariant to patient identity are powerful in arrhythmia detection. We made our code available in: https://github.com/mandiehyewon/goodviews_ecg.git

--- Researcher A ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b (PCLR): Introduces a contrastive pre-training method for 12-lead ECGs using 3.2M unlabeled examples, yielding latent representations that improve downstream clinical tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels. Contributes a scalable, self-supervised representation learning approach for high-dimensional physiological signals.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
- PCLR’s ECG latent space can serve as a continuous, low-dimensional phenotype for physiological state. We propose linking this representation to behavioral or environmental time-series data via a cross-modal alignment objective. Specifically, we hypothesize that PCLR embeddings encode cardiac-autonomic state changes that are causally modulated by circadian and activity patterns. The operational connection: use PCLR’s frozen encoder to project raw ECGs into a latent trajectory, then train a lightweight recurrent model to predict the next latent state from activity/circadian features. This forces the integration of physiological representation (PCLR) with external temporal context, creating a testable model of state transition dynamics.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Dataset: Use a subset of the 3.2M ECG corpus where simultaneous wearable actigraphy or timestamped activity logs are available (if missing, explicitly note this as a required resource).
- Measurements: For each patient, compute PCLR embeddings for all ECGs; align with hourly activity counts and circadian phase (from timestamps). 
- Model: Train a sequence-to-sequence predictor (e.g., GRU) that takes activity/circadian features at time t and predicts the PCLR embedding at t+1. Validate via held-out patients and compare against a baseline that ignores activity (autoregressive embedding only).
- Validation: Test if predicted embeddings preserve clinically relevant distances (e.g., nearest-neighbor classification of arrhythmia or ischemia labels using predicted vs. actual embeddings). Also probe whether circadian features improve prediction of embedding drift.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose a cross-disciplinary framework that integrates self-supervised ECG representation learning (PCLR) with temporal behavioral modeling to predict physiological state transitions. By treating PCLR embeddings as a latent cardiac-autonomic phenotype, we train a recurrent model to forecast future embeddings from activity and circadian inputs. This tests whether external behavioral rhythms causally shape the learned ECG manifold, offering a new tool for personalized monitoring and early warning systems. The contribution beyond PCLR alone is a predictive, context-aware model of latent cardiovascular state dynamics, not just static representation.

FINAL IDEA: Integrate PCLR’s ECG latent space with behavioral time-series forecasting to test whether circadian and activity patterns causally drive transitions in cardiac-autonomic state, enabling predictive physiological monitoring beyond static representation learning.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
- Proposed hypothesis: Individual differences in the *efficiency* of prefrontal–amygdala regulation (from Paper A’s neural metric) causally buffer the impact of daily stress (from Paper B’s EMA metric) on working-memory updating over time. Mechanism is operational: the neural regulation index moderates the stress→cognition slope estimated from Paper B’s repeated-measures design. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source paper includes both neural and EMA data in the same sample; the moderation path is our proposal, not a claim from either paper.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
- Sample: 120 healthy adults aged 50–70 (to match Paper B’s aging focus and ensure variability in stress and cognition).  
- Phase 1 (lab): Administer Paper A’s emotion-regulation fMRI task; extract per-person prefrontal–amygdala connectivity during reappraisal vs. passive viewing (regression beta).  
- Phase 2 (field): 21 days of Paper B’s EMA (5 prompts/day: stressor occurrence, intensity, affect). Concurrent daily 2-minute working-memory updating task (from Paper B) delivered via smartphone at fixed evening time.  
- Analysis: Multilevel model: daily updating accuracy ~ daily stressor intensity × neural regulation index + covariates (age, baseline updating). Validate neural metric by test–retest in 20 participants.  
- Predicted pattern: For high neural regulation, stress→updating slope ≈ 0; for low regulation, negative slope.  

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
We propose a neuroecological study integrating an fMRI marker of prefrontal–amygdala emotion-regulation efficiency with a 21-day EMA protocol of daily stress and working-memory updating in older adults. The neural marker is hypothesized to moderate the daily stress–cognition coupling, such that individuals with stronger regulation show resilience. This would extend Paper A’s lab-based neural findings to real-life cognitive dynamics and extend Paper B’s stress–cognition link by identifying a neural protective factor.

FINAL IDEA: A longitudinal neuroecological design testing whether individual differences in prefrontal–amygdala regulation efficiency moderate the daily impact of stress on working-memory updating in older adults.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
- Adopt: Paper-b’s PCLR encoder as a feature extractor for serial ECGs; Paper-c’s AI-screen positive/negative as a clinically meaningful endpoint.
- Reject: Researcher B’s use of PCLR embeddings as a direct “cardiac-autonomic phenotype” without empirical grounding; embeddings are not a priori interpretable.
- Qualify: Instead of assuming embeddings encode contractile changes, we propose a supervised mapping from embedding trajectories to paper-c’s future-dysfunction risk. The causal/operational link: PCLR embeddings capture subtle, distributed ECG features that paper-c’s static model uses only implicitly; temporal changes in these embeddings should precede a positive screen. Thus, we model PCLR embedding drift as an early-warning signal for paper-c’s validated endpoint.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Data: Serial 12-lead ECGs (≥2 per patient, ≥6 months apart) from a cohort with baseline EF>35% and follow-up echocardiograms or paper-c labels. If paper-c’s Mayo data unavailable, explicitly note missing resource and propose a multi-site ECG repository with documented EF outcomes.

Label each time step by paper-c’s AI-screen result (positive if model output exceeds validated threshold; negative otherwise). Primary outcome: first positive screen within 2 years.
- Model: Train a recurrent neural network (GRU) on embedding sequences to predict time-to-positive screen (survival analysis with discrete time). Baseline 1: paper-c’s static AI model on latest ECG. Baseline 2: logistic regression on latest PCLR embedding only. Baseline 3: change in raw ECG voltage features.
- Validation: 5-fold cross-validation by patient; report time-dependent AUC and integrated Brier score. Probe embedding dimensions most predictive of transition; test if embedding drift magnitude correlates with time-to-positive screen using Cox regression on drift norm.

We propose a dynamic risk model that integrates self-supervised ECG representations (PCLR) with a clinically validated AI screening endpoint for left ventricular dysfunction (paper-c). By modeling trajectories of PCLR embeddings from serial ECGs, we test whether latent-state drift forecasts future positive screens earlier than a single static ECG. This yields a time-to-event warning system that improves temporal precision over paper-c’s static screening and adds clinical interpretability to PCLR’s latent space. The contribution beyond either paper alone is a trajectory-based forecasting model linking unsupervised representation learning to an actionable, validated cardiac outcome.

FINAL IDEA: A recurrent model on PCLR embedding trajectories forecasts paper-c’s validated future left-ventricular-dysfunction screen positivity, creating a dynamic early-warning system neither static AI screening nor representation learning alone provides.
